items.title: 11.7.2 Carbocation stability and the inductive effect of alkyl groups

blocks.text: The reactions of alkenes mostly proceed through carbocations, so their stability must be understood before the addition reactions. A carbocation is an alkyl group with a single positive charge on one of its carbon atoms. A carbocation bonded to H only is a methyl carbocation; bonded to one carbon (alkyl substituent) it is primary (1 degree); bonded directly to two carbons, secondary (2 degree); bonded directly to three carbons, tertiary (3 degree).

blocks.title: Inductive effect
blocks.text: The polarisation of a sigma bond by the electron-withdrawing or electron-donating effect of adjacent groups or atoms is the inductive effect. Electron-donating species such as alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect (+I); electron-withdrawing species such as a halogen atom have a negative inductive effect (-I).

Alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon are electron-donating; because of its positive charge a carbocation is an electrophile. The inductive effect is shown by arrowheads on the bonds, the alkyl groups pushing electrons towards the positive carbon (Figure 11.11). As a result the carbocation becomes less positively charged and energetically more stable, so stability increases with the number of alkyl groups through their +I effect: the tertiary carbocation, with three electron-donating alkyl groups, is the most stable.

blocks.alt: Four carbocations in a row separated by less-than signs: methyl (C+ with three H), 1 degree (one R with an arrowhead on the R-C bond pointing to C+), 2 degree (two R) and 3 degree (three R), each labelled with the number of alkyl groups donating electrons. A red arrow below reads Stability increases.
